id.label: Preset ID
id.short: Unique name for this preset; used in URLs, the CLI and `?preset=`.
id.notes:
Letters, digits, `-` and `_`. It is the file name in `storage/presets/`
and the default API model name when no alias is set. Renaming is not
editing: change the id by duplicating, then deleting the old preset, so the
running instance and its log stay attached to the name they started with.

name.label: Display name
name.short: Human-readable name shown in the dashboard.
name.notes: Free text. It is only for display, so clients never see it.

enabled.label: Enabled
enabled.short: Only enabled presets are offered to clients and can be started.
enabled.notes:
A disabled preset is parked: it is not in `/v1/models`, the proxy refuses
it, and it can't be started or set to start at boot. Its settings are kept,
and it can still be edited, duplicated or deleted. Use this for
experiments, old versions you might go back to, or presets that need the
whole machine. That way an agent framework that picks "the first model in
the list" never lands on them. Disabling a running preset stops it first.

engine_id.label: Engine
engine_id.short: Which llama-server build runs this preset.
engine_id.notes:
Engines are defined in `config/engines/`. Each one names a `llama-server`
binary and the defaults that apply to it. Use a different engine when you
need a fork or a specially built version, for example the ngrams build for
MTP drafting. Help text and allowed values in this form are written for
the n-gram/MTP build. Another engine may accept different values for
`spec_type` or the cache types.

binary_path.label: Binary override
binary_path.short: Use a different llama-server binary than the engine's.
binary_path.notes:
Leave this empty. It exists for one-off tests of a fresh build without
creating a new engine. LlmChooser sets `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` to the binary's
directory, so shared libraries built next to it are found.

model_path.label: Model
model_path.notes:
Pick a model from the scan. For split models (`-00001-of-00003.gguf`),
choose the first part; llama.cpp finds the rest. The Models tab shows how
big the model is, what its maximum context is, and what the KV cache will
cost before you commit to a preset.

mmproj_path.label: Vision projector
mmproj_path.short: Multimodal projector file; enables image input.
mmproj_path.notes:
A vision model ships as two files: the language model and a small
"mmproj" file that turns images into embeddings the model can read. Without
it the model is text-only, even when it was trained on images. The mmproj
must come from the same model family and release as the main model, since
mismatched projectors load fine but produce nonsense. It adds a few hundred
MiB to a couple of GiB of memory and is offloaded to the GPU by default.
Leave it empty if you don't send images; that saves memory and load time.

model_draft_path.label: Draft model
model_draft_path.short: Small model or MTP head used for speculative decoding.
model_draft_path.notes:
Speculative decoding: a cheap model guesses the next few tokens, and the
big model checks all the guesses in one pass. Correct guesses come almost
free, so generation gets faster with **identical** output, because the big
model still decides every token. The draft must share the main model's
tokenizer (same family). For `spec_type = draft-mtp`, this is the model's
own multi-token-prediction head file rather than a separate model. See
Speculative decoding below. The draft also needs memory for its weights
and KV cache.

ttl_seconds.label: Idle unload after (s)
ttl_seconds.short: Stop the instance after this many idle seconds (0 = never).
ttl_seconds.notes:
**Not enforced yet.** LlmChooser records the last-used time on every
proxied request, but there is no idle-stop job yet (see DEPLOY.md). Once
there is one, this frees memory from models you forgot about, which is the
behaviour llama-swap has today.

assigned_port.label: Fixed port
assigned_port.upstream_default: 8080 (LlmChooser instead picks a free port in 5800–5900)
assigned_port.short: Pin this preset to a port; empty = pick automatically.
assigned_port.notes:
Only needed when a client talks to llama-server directly instead of
through `/v1`. Normally leave it empty and use the proxy.

notes.label: Notes
notes.short: Free-form notes; not used by anything.
notes.notes:
Record why the preset exists and what you tuned. Your future self will want
it.

## Context & memory

ctx_size.label: Context size
ctx_size.short: Size of the prompt context in tokens (0 = model's trained maximum).
ctx_size.notes:
The context window holds the conversation, meaning the system prompt,
history, tool output, and the reply being generated. When it fills,
generation stops (or old tokens are dropped, see Context shift).

Cost: the KV cache grows linearly with context, and at long contexts it can
exceed the model weights. The Models tab shows the cost per 1K tokens.
Roughly, KV bytes ≈ ctx × layers × KV heads × head dim × 2 (K and V) ×
bytes per element. GQA models (few KV heads) are cheap, older full-attention
models are expensive.

With `parallel` > 1 the context is shared across slots: each slot gets
ctx_size ÷ parallel unless the build sizes a shared pool (see Parallel).

0 means "whatever the model was trained for", read from the GGUF. That is
a reasonable default on a host with enough memory for it. Lower it
to fit a bigger model, or to run several presets at once. Going above the
trained length requires RoPE/YaRN scaling (extra flags) and degrades
quality.

n_predict.label: Max reply tokens
n_predict.short: Maximum tokens to generate per reply (-1 = unlimited).
n_predict.notes:
A server-side cap. Clients normally send their own `max_tokens`, which takes
priority per request. A cap here guards against runaway generation (a model
stuck in a loop fills the whole context). With reasoning models, remember
that thinking tokens count, so a low cap can cut a model off mid-thought
with no answer at all.

batch_size.label: Logical batch
batch_size.short: Max tokens submitted to the model per decode call.
batch_size.notes:
Prompt processing (reading your input) handles tokens in batches. This is
the logical batch, the most tokens the server hands over at once. It must be
≥ ubatch_size. Raising it rarely helps on its own. Embedding and reranking
models need batch ≥ the longest input. Leave it at 2048.

ubatch_size.label: Physical batch
ubatch_size.short: Tokens actually computed together on the device.
ubatch_size.notes:
The micro-batch the GPU really computes in one go. Larger values speed up
prompt processing, especially on long prompts, at the cost of a bigger
compute buffer (hundreds of MiB to a few GiB). On an iGPU, 1024–2048
often gives noticeably faster prompt reading; measure with a long prompt
before and after. It has no effect on generation speed.

flash_attn.label: Flash attention
flash_attn.short: Fused attention kernel: on, off, or auto.
flash_attn.notes:
Flash attention computes attention without building the full attention
matrix. It uses less memory, is usually faster, and is **required** for a
quantized V cache (cache_type_v other than f16/bf16/f32). `auto` turns it on
when the backend supports it for this model. Set `off` only to work around
a backend bug (garbled output or a crash that goes away without it).

cache_type_k.label: KV cache type (K)
cache_type_k.short: Data type for the attention key cache.
cache_type_k.notes:
Quantizing the KV cache halves (q8_0) or quarters (q4_0) its memory, which
means much longer contexts for the same RAM. Quality: q8_0 is practically
lossless and the usual choice. q4_0/q4_1/iq4_nl are noticeably worse on long
or precise tasks (code, retrieval from deep in context). K is more
sensitive than V, so if you go below q8_0, keep K at q8_0 and lower only V.
Quantized types can be a little slower on some backends.

cache_type_v.label: KV cache type (V)
cache_type_v.short: Data type for the attention value cache.
cache_type_v.notes:
Same choices as K. Quantized V **requires flash attention**, and the server
refuses to start without it. V tolerates quantization better than K:
`K=q8_0, V=q4_0` is a reasonable memory-saving combination, while
`K=q8_0, V=q8_0` is the safe default for long contexts.

parallel.label: Parallel slots
parallel.short: Number of requests served concurrently (-1 = auto).
parallel.notes:
Each slot is an independent conversation, and the context is divided among
the slots: with a 262144 context and 4 slots each conversation gets only
65536 tokens, and it stops when its own slot is full even if the total is
not. Several clients, or an agent plus
a subagent, can generate at once, and continuous batching interleaves
them. Total throughput rises, but each stream slows down.

How context is shared (from this build's source):

- `ctx_size` is the **total** KV cache for all slots together. Memory
  does not grow with `parallel`.
- With an explicit `parallel` N, each slot gets ctx_size ÷ N (rounded to a
  multiple of 256). So 4 slots on 128K give 32K per conversation.
- With `parallel = -1` (auto), the server uses **4 slots and one unified KV
  pool**. Every slot can use up to the whole context, but they share it,
  so a long conversation in one slot leaves less for the others.
- No slot ever exceeds the model's trained context.

1 suits a single user and MTP/speculative drafting (the ngrams preset
uses 1). Use 2–4 when several agents hit the same model.

no_context_shift.label: Disable context shift
no_context_shift.short: Stop with an error when the context fills, instead of dropping old tokens.
no_context_shift.notes:
With context shift on, a full context discards the oldest tokens (after the
system prompt) and keeps generating. The conversation continues, but the
model silently forgets its beginning, which is a frequent source of
confusing behaviour in agents. With it off (our default and llama.cpp's),
the request ends with a clear "context full" error, and the client can
summarise or truncate on purpose. Keep it disabled.

threads.label: CPU threads
threads.notes:
This only matters for the parts running on the CPU (layers not offloaded,
or a pure CPU run). With everything on the GPU it barely matters. When the
CPU does matter, the best value is usually the number of **physical**
cores, not logical threads. More can be slower because of
memory-bandwidth contention.

## GPU

n_gpu_layers.label: GPU layers
n_gpu_layers.short: Layers to put on the GPU: a number, `auto`, or `all`.
n_gpu_layers.notes:
`all` puts every layer on the GPU (fastest, needs the most VRAM). `auto` lets
llama.cpp fit as many as memory allows. A number offloads exactly that
many, and the rest run on the CPU, much slower. On a unified-memory host,
RAM and VRAM are the same unified pool, so `all` is almost always right. Lower it only
when memory is short and you accept a slowdown.

split_mode.label: Multi-GPU split
split_mode.short: How to divide the model across GPUs.
split_mode.notes:
Irrelevant with one GPU. `layer` gives whole layers to each GPU,
which is pipelined and the safe choice. `row` splits each matrix across GPUs
and only helps with fast interconnects. `tensor` is newer tensor parallelism.
`none` uses only `main_gpu`.

tensor_split.label: GPU split ratios
tensor_split.short: Share of the model per GPU, e.g. `3,1`.
tensor_split.notes:
Multi-GPU only. Ratios, not absolute sizes: `3,1` puts ¾ on GPU 0. Leave it
empty on a single-GPU host.

main_gpu.label: Main GPU
main_gpu.notes:
Multi-GPU only. Leave it at 0 on a single-GPU host.

## Sampling

These are server defaults. Most OpenAI-compatible clients send their own
temperature and top_p per request, and those override what is set here.
Model cards often state recommended values; use them.

temp.label: Temperature
temp.short: Randomness of token choice (0 = always most likely).
temp.notes:
Temperature divides the model's scores before picking a token. Low values
(0.1–0.4) are focused and repeatable, good for code and tool calls. Around
0.7–1.0 they are varied and creative. Above 1.2 output gets incoherent.
Reasoning models are usually tuned for 0.6–1.0 and get worse at 0, getting
stuck in loops. Follow the model card.

top_k.label: Top-K
top_k.short: Only consider the K most likely tokens (0 = off).
top_k.notes:
A hard cap on candidates per step. A blunt filter: min_p does the same job
more adaptively. Note the preset default is 20 (Qwen recommendation), not
llama.cpp's 40.

top_p.label: Top-P (nucleus)
top_p.short: Keep the smallest set of tokens whose probability sums to P (1.0 = off).
top_p.notes:
Cuts off the long tail of unlikely tokens. 0.9–0.95 is typical. Combined
with min_p it is mostly redundant. Many guides now suggest top_p = 1.0 plus
min_p alone.

min_p.label: Min-P
min_p.short: Drop tokens less likely than P × the top token's probability (0 = off).
min_p.notes:
An adaptive cutoff. When the model is confident, few alternatives
survive; when it is unsure, many do. That keeps output coherent at higher
temperatures. 0.05–0.1 is a good general setting.

repeat_penalty.label: Repeat penalty
repeat_penalty.notes:
The old anti-repetition tool. Values above 1.0 make recently seen tokens
less likely, but they also punish legitimate repetition (code syntax,
names, JSON keys), so tool calls and code get worse. Leave it at 1.0 for
modern models. Use presence_penalty if a model loops.

presence_penalty.label: Presence penalty
presence_penalty.short: Flat penalty on any token already used (OpenAI semantics).
presence_penalty.notes:
Pushes the model toward new words and topics. Qwen recommends 0–1.5 to
reduce endless repetition in long thinking. Start at 0 and raise it only if
you see loops.

frequency_penalty.label: Frequency penalty
frequency_penalty.short: Penalty growing with how often a token has appeared.
frequency_penalty.notes: Like presence penalty, but scaled by count. It is rarely needed; leave it at 0.

seed.label: Seed
seed.notes:
A fixed seed gives repeatable output for the same prompt and settings,
which is useful when comparing presets. It is only repeatable with the
same build, slot, and batch configuration.

## Speculative decoding

spec_type.label: Speculative method
spec_type.short: How draft tokens are produced for speculative decoding.
spec_type.notes:
All methods keep the output identical to normal decoding. They only change
speed, which depends on how often the drafts are accepted (shown in the
server log). Families:

- `draft-simple`: a separate small model from the same family (`model_draft_path`). Classic speculative decoding.
- `draft-mtp`: the model's own multi-token-prediction head. Models like Qwen3-Next / DeepSeek ship one; it is very accurate and cheap. The ngram engine's preset uses this with `spec_draft_n_max 2`.
- `draft-eagle3`: an EAGLE-3 draft head trained for the specific model.
- `ngram-*`: no draft model at all. Guesses come from repeating sequences already in the context. They are excellent for code editing, rewriting, and quoting (the output copies the input), and do nothing for fresh prose. They cost almost no memory.
- `draft-dflash`: a small block-diffusion draft model trained for one specific target (e.g. `Qwen3-4B-DFlash` for Qwen3-4B), given as `model_draft_path`. It reads the target's hidden states and emits a whole block of draft tokens in one pass, rather than one at a time. Upstream example: `spec_draft_n_max 15`, `flash_attn on`.
- `draft-dspark`: DFlash plus a small "Markov head" that conditions each position on the previous token, which recovers some left-to-right accuracy. The draft is a DeepSpec checkpoint for one target. Upstream example: `spec_draft_n_max 7`. Only Qwen3-backbone drafts are supported so far.
- For both, `spec_draft_n_max` is clamped to the draft's trained block size, so setting it higher does nothing.

The field accepts a comma-separated list to combine methods. Expect
roughly 1.3–2.5× faster generation when acceptance is high, and possibly a
small slowdown when it is low.

spec_draft_n_max.label: Max draft tokens
spec_draft_n_max.short: How many tokens to guess ahead per step.
spec_draft_n_max.notes:
More guesses mean bigger wins when they're right and more wasted work when
they're wrong. MTP heads are accurate for only 1–3 tokens (use 2). Small
draft models are good for 4–8. Ngram methods on repetitive text can use
16+. Note the preset default is 16 versus llama.cpp's 3, which suits
ngram/draft models; **lower it for MTP**.

## Chat

alias.label: API model name
alias.short: Name clients use in `"model"`; empty = preset id.
alias.notes:
What `/v1/models` lists and what a client puts in its `model` field to
reach this preset through the proxy. It must be unique across presets.
Use a stable name (e.g. `qwen-coder`) so clients don't need reconfiguring
when you swap the underlying file.

jinja.label: Use model chat template
jinja.short: Format chats with the model's own Jinja template.
jinja.notes:
The template turns messages into the exact token layout the model was
trained on. It is required for tool calling and reasoning models. Disable
it only for old models with broken templates.

reasoning_effort.label: Reasoning effort
reasoning_effort.short: How hard reasoning models think before answering.
reasoning_effort.notes:
For models that support it (gpt-oss, some Qwen/DeepSeek variants), this
trades answer quality against time and tokens. `low` is fast and fine for
chat. `high`/`max` suits hard maths and code, but can think for thousands
of tokens. Models without an effort control ignore it. Clients can usually
override it per request.

## Other

extra_flags.label: Extra flags
extra_flags.short: Any other llama-server options, appended to the command line.
extra_flags.notes:
This is the escape hatch for everything without its own field, e.g.
`--fit off --lazy-mode on --metrics`, `--rope-scaling yarn`,
`--threads-batch 16`. Not allowed: `--host`, `--port` (LlmChooser owns
them). If you find yourself using a flag in many presets, ask for it to
become a real field.
